content:
Builders in Mylapore: the decision before the drawings

Mylapore is one of Chennai's oldest neighbourhoods, built around the Kapaleeshwarar Temple and its tank.

The streets around the temple, and the older lanes beyond them, still have traditional houses: a thinnai at the front, a long plan running deep into the plot, sometimes an open courtyard in the middle, and side walls that touch or are shared with the house next door. Many have Madras terrace roofs on timber beams.

Most of these houses have also passed down through a generation or two. That is the first thing we ask about in Mylapore. Not the plot size. Who owns it.

Ownership comes first

An old family house often has several owners: siblings, cousins, sometimes heirs who live abroad. Every one of them has to agree, and sign, before a building approval, a bank loan or a joint development agreement can go ahead.

Before we discuss design, we check:

  • The parent document and the chain of title, back far enough to be sure.
  • Whether the property has been partitioned, or is still held jointly.
  • A legal heir certificate where the last owner has passed away.
  • Patta and property tax in names that match the deed.
  • Any tenants or occupants who will need to move out.

This is slow work. It is also the step that most often decides whether the project happens at all.

Rebuild or joint development?

In Mylapore, the choice between rebuilding and joint development usually follows from the family, not from the building.

RebuildJoint development
Who pays for constructionYouThe developer
What you getThe whole buildingAn agreed share of the built area, usually flats
Design controlFullLimited to your share
SuitsOne family wanting an independent homeSeveral co-owners who each want a separate flat

Joint development can solve a problem that a rebuild cannot. When four heirs share one house, four flats can be fairer than one home none of them can afford to buy out. Our joint development service explains how we structure these projects. Before signing with anyone, read about the risks landowners should check: delays, approval changes and what happens if the developer stops work.

If one family is keeping the house, a rebuild usually gives a better home. The rest of this page is about doing that well.

The heritage feel of the street

Some buildings and precincts in Mylapore are recognised for their heritage value. If your house, or the street it is on, could fall under heritage rules, confirm with CMDA before planning demolition. We raise this at the document stage, not after.

Even where no rule applies, many owners want the new house to sit comfortably on an old street. Things we often discuss:

  • Salvage before demolition. Old teak doors, carved pillars, window grilles and timber beams can be removed carefully and reused. They have to be taken out before the machines arrive, not picked from the debris.
  • A thinnai or deep verandah at the front, which also shades the house.
  • A courtyard or central light well. On a long, narrow plot it brings light and air into the middle rooms, which is why the old houses had one.
  • Traditional floor tiles or lime-plaster finishes in a few rooms, with modern services hidden behind them.

Demolition next to an old neighbour

Many Mylapore houses were built in lime mortar, with walls that touch the neighbour's. Taking one down without damaging the other is careful, mostly manual work.

  • We photograph and note the neighbour's walls before we start, and share the record with them.
  • Shared or touching walls are taken down by hand. Whether a shared wall stays is a structural decision, made with the neighbour's agreement.
  • Where the neighbour's house depends on support from yours, we brace it before removing anything.
  • Debris goes out in small loads, because lanes near the temple are narrow and busy.

The temple calendar matters too. During the Panguni festival the streets around the temple fill with devotees, and we plan deliveries and noisy work around those days.

When you compare builders in Mylapore, ask how they would take down your side wall, and whether they have worked beside an occupied old house before. A builder used only to open plots will often price the demolition as a single line. On these streets it is several separate jobs, each with its own risk.

What a rebuild in Mylapore costs

Our packages are priced per sq ft of built-up area: Basic ₹2,199, Standard ₹2,399, Premium ₹2,699 and Ultra Luxury ₹3,199.

A worked example. A rebuilt family home of 2,400 sq ft built-up at Premium comes to about ₹64.8 lakh (2,400 × ₹2,699).

Approvals, demolition, soil test, compound wall, sump and interiors are extra. In Mylapore, also allow for careful salvage of old timber and its restoration, and for any legal work needed to settle ownership first.

How Hunter Property handles a build in Mylapore

Mylapore is a short drive from our Royapettah branch.

  1. Site visit. We walk the house with you, note what is worth saving and look at the neighbours' walls.
  2. Document check. Title chain, heirs, partition and patta, before design.
  3. Design that suits the plot's long shape and the street.
  4. Approval with the Greater Chennai Corporation, or CMDA where the building's size requires it, including any heritage clearance that applies.
  5. Salvage, demolition and construction in stages, with daily progress reports and photos.
  6. Stage-wise payments as each stage is completed and checked.

Talk to us about your Mylapore house

Tell us how many owners the property has, the plot size and whether you are leaning towards a rebuild or joint development. We will look at both honestly and give you the numbers for each.
faqTitle: Old houses in Mylapore: questions owners ask

faqs.question: Our Mylapore house has several owners. Can we still rebuild?
faqs.answer: Yes, if every owner agrees and signs. Before a building approval or loan, the title has to be clear: partition or joint ownership settled, legal heir papers in place and patta matching the deed. We check these before design.

faqs.question: Is joint development better than rebuilding for an old Mylapore house?
faqs.answer: It depends on the family. Joint development suits several co-owners who each want a flat and do not want to fund construction. Rebuilding suits one family that wants an independent home with full design control.

faqs.question: Can we reuse old doors, pillars or beams from our house?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Teak doors, pillars, grilles and beams can be removed by hand before demolition, then restored and fitted in the new house. Salvage has to be planned before demolition starts, not after.

faqs.question: Is my Mylapore house a heritage building?
faqs.answer: Most are not formally listed, but some buildings and precincts in Mylapore are recognised for heritage value. If there is any chance yours is one of them, confirm with CMDA before planning demolition. We raise this during the document check.

faqs.question: How do you demolish a house that shares a wall with the neighbour?
faqs.answer: By hand near the shared wall, after photographing the neighbour's side and agreeing the plan with them. If their house relies on support from yours, we brace it first. Whether the shared wall stays is a structural decision.

faqs.question: What does rebuilding a house in Mylapore cost?
faqs.answer: A 2,400 sq ft home at our Premium package of ₹2,699 per sq ft comes to about ₹64.8 lakh. Approvals, demolition, soil test, compound wall, sump, interiors and any salvage restoration are extra.
